questions.prompt: What is the main reason for Earth’s seasons?
options: Earth’s tilt as it travels around the Sun
questions.explanation: The tilt changes the angle of sunlight and the number of daylight hours through the year.

questions.prompt: When the northern half of Earth has summer, what season does the southern half have?
questions.explanation: The northern half leans towards the Sun while the southern half leans away, so their summer and winter are opposite.

questions.prompt: Which pair helps explain summer warmth?
options: Longer days and more direct sunlight
Shorter days and less direct sunlight
A bigger Moon and darker nights
The Sun coming closer to only one country
questions.explanation: More direct sunlight and more daylight hours help the ground warm up.

title: Why is summer warmer than winter?

sources.name: NASA Space Place — What causes the seasons?

practice: Try Science Quiz for more questions about Earth and space.

sections.title: Earth spins with a little lean
sections.html:
Imagine a spinning globe. A line through its middle, from the North Pole to the South Pole, is its axis. It is an imaginary line, not a real pole running through Earth.

Earth spins on this line as it travels around the Sun. The line is tilted: Earth has a little lean.

That lean is the main reason we have seasons. At one part of the year, the northern half of Earth leans towards the Sun. About six months later, the southern half does.

sections.title: What does “hemisphere” mean?
sections.html:
A hemisphere is half of a sphere. Here, it means half of Earth.

The Northern Hemisphere is the half north of the equator, the imaginary line around Earth’s middle. The Southern Hemisphere is the half south of it.

When the northern half leans towards the Sun, the southern half leans away. That is why their summer and winter happen at opposite times.

sections.title: Two things help summer feel warmer
sections.html:
1. Sunlight hits more directly. Picture a torch shining straight down on a table. Its light makes a small, bright patch. Tilt the torch and the light spreads over a larger patch. Sunlight arriving at a low angle is spread out too.
  2. The days are longer. There are more hours of daylight for the ground to warm up.

These changes help explain summer warmth. A particular summer day can still be cold or rainy: daily weather can vary.

sections.title: One planet, opposite seasons
sections.html:
Compare the two halves of Earth
Northern halfSouthern half
Summer: longer days, more direct sunlightWinter: shorter days, less direct sunlight
Winter: shorter days, less direct sunlightSummer: longer days, more direct sunlight

sections.title: Is summer just when Earth is closer to the Sun?
sections.html:
No. Earth’s distance from the Sun changes a little during the year, but it does not explain why one half of Earth has summer while the other has winter.

The tilt explains that difference. It changes the sunlight reaching each half through the year.

sections.title: Look for a small clue outdoors
sections.html:
Over a few weeks, notice whether it gets dark earlier or later. Those changing daylight hours are one clue to the seasonal pattern.

You do not need to look at the Sun. Simply noticing when daylight ends is enough.

description: Earth leans as it travels around the Sun. That small tilt changes how much sunlight reaches us—and how long it stays light each day.
